Heavy Flooding Disrupts Construction Materials Supply in Lebanon

BEIRUT, June 13 – Severe flooding triggered by days of torrential rain has struck Lebanon’s construction materials industry, inundating cement plants, quarries and key transport routes across the country, company officials and industry sources said Thursday.

Production at several concrete and cement facilities, including Holcim Liban SAL’s main plant in Chekka, has been suspended due to rising water levels and damage to access roads, the company said in a statement. “The safety of our employees is our priority,” Holcim Liban SAL’s site manager, Michel Farhat, told reporters. “Floodwaters have reached the plant perimeter, forcing us to halt operations and evacuate non-essential personnel.”

Industry representatives reported that at least three major quarries in the Mount Lebanon area were inaccessible as rivers overflowed, with some equipment submerged. “It’s the worst flooding we’ve seen in over a decade. Deliveries have ground to a halt,” said Rami Haddad, secretary of the Lebanese Construction Materials Association.

The Ministry of Public Works said more than 50 kilometers of major highways and rural roads used for transporting aggregates and finished cement products were blocked or washed out in multiple locations, leaving trucks stranded and delaying shipments. The coastal port of Tripoli, an important entry point for construction imports, remained operational but was experiencing disruptions due to the closure of inland routes.

Early estimates from the association suggest daily cement output has fallen by up to 70 percent since Monday. Contractors reported immediate shortages of concrete and other materials at several building sites.

“We are coordinating with authorities to restore access as soon as possible,” said Nada Khoury, spokesperson for Beirut ReadyMix, another affected producer. “But with the rain still coming down, it is unclear when normal distribution can resume.”

Meteorologists forecast further heavy rain through Saturday, raising concerns that floodwaters could rise further in the coming days.
